tur52-0: What is fibromyalgia, how is it recognised and how is it treated? How do you start exercise, the only treatment with a strong recommendation? The 2016 diagnostic criteria, a comparison of EULAR and NICE, a short history, six home exercises, a tai chi video and warning signs.
tur52-1: A condition with widespread, lasting pain in many parts of the body, fatigue and unrefreshing sleep. The pain is real; fibromyalgia does not damage muscles or joints, and it is thought that the way the nervous system processes pain has changed. Exercise is the treatment with the strongest evidence.
tur52-2: How common fibromyalgia is in the general population (about 1.8%); much more common in women
tur52-3: The only treatment with a strong recommendation in the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) recommendations
tur52-5: The diagnosis is based on symptoms lasting at least 3 months and on assessing the widespread pain and accompanying symptoms at an examination. Conditions that can cause similar symptoms (such as thyroid disorders, rheumatic diseases and vitamin deficiencies) are looked for with an examination and, if needed, blood tests. However, according to the diagnostic criteria updated in 2016, fibromyalgia can occur together with another condition; having another diagnosis does not invalidate a diagnosis of fibromyalgia. There is no single blood test or scan that makes the diagnosis.
tur52-8: There is no single blood test or scan that shows fibromyalgia; the diagnosis is made by assessing the symptoms together. The criteria revised in 2016 use two scales.
tur52-10: Counts how many of 19 body areas are painful (0–19 points).
tur52-12: Scores the severity of symptoms such as fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and difficulty with attention or memory (0–12 points).
tur52-14: A Widespread Pain Index of 7 or more and a Symptom Severity score of 5 or more, or a Widespread Pain Index of 4–6 and a Symptom Severity score of 9 or more; pain in at least 4 of 5 body regions; symptoms present for at least 3 months. The diagnosis can be made regardless of whether other conditions are present.
tur52-15: The criteria are a guiding framework; looking for other conditions that can cause similar symptoms, and making the diagnosis, are done by a physician.
tur52-17: Widespread muscle pain has been described for more than a century; over time both its name and its diagnostic criteria have changed. Studies over the last twenty years have clarified the place of exercise in treatment.
tur52-18: Gowers used the term "fibrositis" for this kind of widespread pain, believing the muscles were inflamed; later tissue studies did not confirm this inflammation.
tur52-19: The term "fibromyalgia" was used by Hench; the first diagnostic criteria were proposed in 1977 and 1981.
tur52-20: The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) criteria: widespread pain together with pain on pressure at at least 11 of 18 tender points on the body. These criteria were an important step towards official recognition, but were later criticised as impractical in everyday use.
tur52-21: The ACR's new criteria replaced the tender point examination with the Widespread Pain Index and the Symptom Severity Scale.
tur52-22: The criteria were revised: pain in at least 4 of 5 regions is required, and the diagnosis can be made regardless of whether other conditions are present.
tur52-23: The European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) updated its recommendations after reviewing 107 systematic reviews with experts from 12 European countries: exercise was the only treatment to receive a strong recommendation.
tur52-24: A Cochrane review covering 13 trials and 839 people: aerobic exercise probably improved quality of life; it was also found that it may slightly improve pain and daily function (certainty of evidence between low and moderate).
tur52-25: In a study of 226 people (BMJ), tai chi gave as much benefit as aerobic exercise or more.
tur52-26: NICE, the body that issues national health guidelines in England, published its guideline on chronic primary pain, which includes fibromyalgia: a supervised group exercise programme was recommended; TENS, ultrasound and interferential current were not recommended.
tur52-27: For people with severe pain or sleep problems, a physician may consider some medicines. Ask your physician which is suitable for you; do not stop a medicine you are taking on your own.
tur52-28: The recommendations of the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) (Ann Rheum Dis, 2017) and England's NICE guideline on chronic primary pain (2021), side by side. EULAR divides its recommendations into "strong" and "weak"; the NICE guideline treats fibromyalgia as a type of chronic primary pain. Treatment is chosen for each person.
tur52-30: The only treatment with a strong recommendation.
tur52-31: A supervised group exercise programme should be offered.
tur52-32: Tai chi, yoga and qigong (weak recommendation).
tur52-33: Cognitive behavioural therapy, mindfulness-based practices and multicomponent programmes (weak recommendation).
tur52-34: Acceptance and commitment therapy or cognitive behavioural therapy may be considered.
tur52-36: Acupuncture, water-based and spa therapy (weak recommendation).
tur52-37: Under certain conditions, a single course of acupuncture or dry needling may be considered.
tur52-38: In Türkiye only authorised physicians may perform acupuncture and dry needling.
tur52-40: Massage and biofeedback are not recommended (weak); chiropractic is strongly not recommended.
tur52-43: TENS, ultrasound and interferential current are not recommended because there is no evidence of benefit.
tur52-44: Some medicines received a weak recommendation for severe pain or sleep problems; strong opioids and cortisone are strongly not recommended.
tur52-45: Some antidepressants may be considered; it is recommended not to start new treatment with paracetamol, anti-inflammatory painkillers, opioids or epilepsy medicines, including gabapentinoids.
tur52-46: The two guidelines reach different conclusions on medicines. Ask your physician which is suitable for you; do not stop a medicine you are taking on your own.
tur52-47: Sit on the front part of a sturdy chair placed against a wall. Stand up and sit back down with control. If it is hard, support yourself with your hands on your knees or on the armrests.

tur52-49: Yes, but by adjusting the dose. A slight increase in the first weeks is usual and generally eases as the body adapts. If the pain is clearly worse the next day, reduce the duration and intensity at the next session; do not stop completely. If the pain does not ease within a few days, or if there is swelling or a new pain, talk to your physician or physiotherapist.
tur52-50: It is usually a long-term condition, and symptoms can come and go. With regular exercise, a sleep routine and pain-coping skills, symptoms can ease for many people.
tur52-51: The following may point to a problem other than fibromyalgia, or to an emergency.
tur52-52: Thoughts of harming yourself, or deep hopelessness
tur52-53: A new problem with bladder or bowel control, or numbness between the legs (with or without leg symptoms)
tur52-54: A new, severe headache, jaw pain or problems with vision
tur52-55: Swelling, redness or warmth in the joints
tur52-57: New pain and stiffness around the shoulders and hips after age 50
tur52-58: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour, or a skin rash

tur52-61: What causes pain on the outer side of the hip, and how is it recognised? For the pain called trochanteric bursitis, is a cortisone injection or exercise better? A comparison of the evidence, a short history, helpful habits, six home exercises and warning signs.
tur52-63: It is most common in middle-aged women but can appear at any age. A direct blow such as a fall, weakness of the hip muscles, long periods of walking or running, and excess weight can set the stage for it; often no clear cause is found.
tur52-64: The diagnosis is mostly made from your history and an examination. A study comparing examination tests with MRI in 65 people with lateral hip pain (BJSM, 2017) looked at which findings are useful. These tests are carried out by a physiotherapist or physician.
tur52-65: Pain on the side of the hip while standing on the painful leg for 30 seconds made a tendon problem very likely (specificity 100%). No pain, however, does not rule the problem out (sensitivity 38%).
tur52-67: No pain when pressing on the bony bump on the side of the hip made a tendon problem less likely (sensitivity 80%). Tenderness on its own, however, does not make the diagnosis (specificity 47%).
tur52-68: If the pain is felt in the groin and hip movements are restricted, hip osteoarthritis is considered; if pain spreading from the lower back to the leg comes with numbness or tingling, a back-related problem is considered.
tur52-69: The LEAP study in Australia tested this question directly. 204 people aged 35–70 who had had lateral hip pain for at least three months, with a tendon problem confirmed by MRI and at least moderate pain, were divided into three groups: eight weeks of education and exercise with a physiotherapist, a single cortisone injection, or information and waiting only.
tur52-71: Lateral hip pain was long called bursitis. Studies over the last decade have shown that the problem usually comes from the tendons on the side of the hip and that exercise supported by education can give more lasting benefit than an injection.
tur52-72: A clinical commentary was published that looks at problems of the lateral hip tendons together with movement mechanics and examination findings, and guides treatment (JOSPT).
tur52-73: Examination tests were compared with MRI in 65 people with lateral hip pain (BJSM): pain while standing on one leg for 30 seconds made a tendon problem very likely, while no tenderness when pressing on the bony bump made it less likely.
tur52-74: The LEAP study of 204 people (BMJ): an education and exercise programme of 14 sessions over 8 weeks gave a higher rate of improvement than both a single cortisone injection and waiting; the difference was still present at 1 year.
tur52-75: A review including five studies (Scientific Reports; three studies, 383 people, in the meta-analysis): exercise was better for function in the short and long term than sham exercise or a wait-and-see approach; for pain it was not different from a cortisone injection. The finding of a higher treatment success rate was based only on the LEAP study. The certainty of evidence was between low and very low.
tur52-76: Treatment options: what does the evidence say?
tur52-77: The findings of the LEAP study (BMJ, 2018) and of a review including five studies with its meta-analysis (Scientific Reports, 2024), side by side. In the meta-analysis the certainty of evidence was between low and very low; treatment is chosen for each person.
tur52-80: 14 sessions over 8 weeks: marked improvement in 77% at week 8 and 79% at 1 year.
tur52-82: Better for function in the short and long term than sham exercise or a wait-and-see approach; no difference in quality of life.
tur52-83: A single injection: marked improvement in 58% at week 8 and 58% at 1 year; at 1 year, pain intensity similar to the exercise group and slightly lower than in those who waited.
tur52-84: Not different from exercise for pain (low certainty); the higher treatment success with exercise rests only on LEAP.
tur52-86: A single information session: marked improvement in 29% at week 8 and 52% at 1 year.
tur52-87: When sitting, keep your knees side by side; avoid low armchairs. Positions that bring the hip inwards can compress the tendons against the bony bump.
tur52-88: If you are overweight, losing weight may reduce the load on the outer side of the hip.
tur52-89: Mild discomfort during the exercises is acceptable; the pain should not be severe or long-lasting. If the pain increases, reduce the number of repetitions or the difficulty. Muscle soreness felt a day or two after exercise is usual; however, if your lateral hip pain is clearly worse the next morning, reduce the load.
tur52-90: Lie on your back with your knees bent. Tie a belt or scarf around your thighs. Gently push your knees outwards just enough to tension the belt and hold; your legs do not move.
tur52-91: In the LEAP study of 204 people, the injection gave a better result than waiting at week eight, but a worse one than education and exercise. After one year there was no longer a significant difference between injection and waiting in the rate of "marked improvement"; pain intensity, however, was slightly lower in the injection group. This is why an injection is not considered the first option; it may be considered for short-term relief if the pain is severe enough to stop you exercising. Make this decision together with your physician.
tur52-92: In a 2024 meta-analysis of five studies, exercise improved daily function more than sham exercise or a wait-and-see approach, in both the short and long term. Its effect on pain was not different from a cortisone injection; however, in one study (LEAP) treatment success was higher with exercise. The certainty of evidence was between low and very low.
tur52-93: Lateral hip pain is usually not an emergency. In the following situations, however, seek help without delay.
tur52-94: If you cannot put weight on your leg after a fall or blow (it may be a fracture)
tur52-95: Hip pain together with a fever, redness or warmth
tur52-96: Back pain together with numbness between the legs, problems with bladder or bowel control, or rapidly increasing leg weakness
tur52-97: Pain that does not ease at rest or at night, unexplained weight loss, or new pain in someone with a history of cancer
tur52-98: Numbness or tingling in the leg
